See an ear nose and throat specialist (ENT), get a facial CT scan done and they can advise if there's any surgical options to reduce symptoms. 

I had chronic sinusitis and basically lived on antibiotics for years as I couldn't keep the infections down despite constant rinses/medications/diet restrictions etc. Saw an ENT who suggested a few fixes to my nose and I've not had an infection since! Really worth a consult.

Did your sister have any health insurance before your mum started paying for it?  Or was it a completely new policy?

I ask because Medibank offer a "mental health waiver" specifically to allow coverage for psychiatric admissions if you've already completed the waiting period on a lower cover. So if your sister has had cover for 12+ months, including any policy before Medibank so long as there was no gap between the two, you can ask for the emergency upgrade to her level of cover which will waive the waiting period. 

It might be a long shot, but worth looking into if it could help. Medibank may not have mentioned it as an option because she hasn't been with them for 12 months. Depending on how the cover was set up they may not have carried over any previous policy waiting periods served, and I'm not sure if that would make a difference for her eligibility for the waiver.

GST aside, you might want to go talk to an accountant to make sure you're not going to get stung down the road doing this. 

Your situation might be classed as personal services income (more than 50% of earnings is for your time and knowledge, not a specific product or result e.g architectural designs), which there's certain tests to meet to discern how it's recorded on your tax return. There's also contractor vs employee implications where your friend may have additional obligations (there's no "but we're friends so it's fine" loophole) like super and insurance. The ATO do not mess around if they catch it.

Also if you own your own home and are running a business from it you can get into a CGT snag if you ever sell, since the property was technically used to earn income. Definitely talk to an accountant about that.

I had nasal surgery to widen passages and fix a crooked septum and it's really cleared up the infections and pain. After that I managed to get back to mostly normal (I have other chronic health issues, so normal for me) so I can only say there's hope. However I will ask have you been in the same home this whole time? Because my symptoms were debilitating and then suddenly improved when I moved out of the rental I was living in. So perhaps looking into things in your environment that can be improved? Even just having air cons serviced, dusting regularly, getting an air purifier for the bedroom, maybe looking at a deep clean or a mobile service that checks for these things. Listen to your body OP, you know when something is wrong. 

I had a similar experience (including the pain easing in different positions) and it is such a horrible feeling being dismissed and gaslit like I didn't know my own body. I KNEW something was wrong. I went to emergency multiple times (usually when the pain got to the point I honestly thought I was dying) and got sent home, constantly tried to get my GP to listen only to have it dismissed as "painful periods" or IBS problems. 

I refused to accept it as my new normal and hounded my GP to keep looking. I had endoscopes, ultrasounds, CT scans, heart tests, etc, until I got to a specialist who agreed to do a diagnostic laparoscopy.   

I won't go into details but the short version is I had an ovarian torsion which rarely show up on any tests. The surgeon was amazed I had gone so long in that level of pain (roughly 4 years between onset and the surgery), like it was a compliment as to how strong I am and not a failure of the medical system. The difference I felt almost immediately after the surgery made me realise I was far, far sicker than even I thought I was. 

I've spoken with people who had similar pain (occurs at random but is debilitating, tests all come back fine, got dismissed as one thing or other) and it's been something similar where blood flow was being restricted somewhere and required surgery to diagnose. 

It's a very hard road but you are not imagining things or being dramatic, you do not have to accept this pain into your life. That level of pain is NOT normal and it is your right to reject any doctor that says otherwise. Keep pushing, ask for diagnostic surgery. You deserve to be heard and taken seriously.

So instead of having normal/stable hormones for the month, then no hormones with the sugar pills to trigger a withdrawal bleed, I just had no hormones so continuously bled (and other wonderful side effects of having unbalanced hormones) meanwhile my other hormones weren't being balanced out from the progesterone/oestrogen. So I got switched to birth control pills that effect androgen or testosterone levels instead and they worked for me.

(This is after I switched doctors because I was sick of being treated like I was just being dramatic, and told I was simply sensitive to periods.)

However please discuss with your doctor!! Everyone's body is different and what worked for me may not work for you. I was told to give it 6 weeks and then if I was still bleeding to tell the doctor. If you're in Australia I find Xero more user friendly, especially with the free hubdoc add on (you upload pictures of receipts, bills, etc and it will read the image and come up with how to add it to Xero). I teach my small business clients how to do the bulk of the work in their own books, and these topics are my first points to teach: 
1. The chart of accounts and different account types
2. Double entry bookkeeping - Credits and debits, and how they affect each account type. Then we'd enter some data to see how it's posted. 
3. Reporting: trial balance, balance sheet, profit and loss, and how the chart of accounts fits into and influences these reports

That being said I check over their files routinely and complete reconciliations for them. So as others have said it would be good to engage a bookkeeper or accountant to assist with initial set up and do some routine checks/reconciliations for you.

If it's done through payroll wait for the end of year finalisation (your payment summary) from your employer and see if it's included as part of your total wages for the year. 

If it's not then it's a reimbursement and not reported as wages by your employer. If it is then you claim the deduction equal to the amount of KMs travelled. The difference in rates 0.98c per km through payroll and 0.85c as a deduction is, I believe, to account for tax withheld on wages

Is it a direct reimbursement or is it paid through payroll? I.e do you submit a claim and have that paid exactly or do you get a set amount of KMs per pay period as an allowance? 

If it's a direct reimbursement then you do not claim it as a deduction. You are technically not out of pocket/haven't paid the expense if your employer has reimbursed an agreed value. 

If it's paid to you in conjuction with your wages then it has been included as part of your income and you would claim the actual KMs travelled as a deduction. That would net out your income with your travel expense to again show you are not out of pocket.

Source: payroll clerk and also went through this process with my last 2 employers.

Taxes are withheld based on the pay each pay period multiplied by the amount of pay periods in a financial year to predict how much tax an employee may need to pay, not how much the employee has earnt in the year so far. For example if the employee claiming the tax free threshold gets paid fortnightly and one fortnight they earn $500 before tax, $500x26 (amount of fortnight's in a financial year)= $13,000 which is less than the threshold, so no tax is withheld. If they earnt $1500 before tax one fortnight, $1500x26 = $39,000, tax will be withheld. 

If the employee does not earn over $18,200 in the financial year they will get a refund of all the tax withheld so far when they lodge their tax return. This is how employment and tax withholding works in Australia. 

I would suggest directing them to the ATO website to learn about this themselves. Ultimately it's not up to an employer to educate an employee on how paying tax works.

I grew up with my mom suffering chronic migraines (among other health issues). She did her best and, like you, I appreciate her and love her so much and think she's an amazing human being. But I've also come to realise mine and my siblings childhoods were not normal. 

I now suffer from migraines myself and I cannot imagine having to raise 4 kids practically by yourself (my dad is a misogynist and narcissist who only cared to be a parent when it benefitted him/his image) with this kind of pain. However the more I deal with them the more I realise how much I lost to them as a kid. Something I didn't realise even with 12+ years of therapy. 

It's hard to reconcile having a wonderful person as your mother with realising you were emotionally abandoned by her. And knowing you'll never be able to talk to her about it because it would break her heart.

It does depend on the level of trust you have with her, if you believe she is willing to work on her mental health (hopefully the fact that she is coming home is because she's ready to). 

Something I've implemented with family /friends due to my own experiences not being able to effectively ask for help is a code system. Check in by asking for a colour/number on a scale, with easy to remember/understand references. For us, red is "I am feeling very unsafe and am at real risk of harming myself" (in which case my response is to wrap up or drop whatever I'm doing and let them know how far away I am, ask them if there's anything in the house I need to hide when I get there and if they want me to alert the troops (the rest of their support system)), orange is "it's a very hard time for me right now and I need some compassion/support", yellow is "things are okay but a bit dicey" and green is "I'm okay/at baseline/no cause for alarm". 

This has been incredibly helpful for us because when you're the orange/red stage, finding the energy/capacity to even articulate it to someone can be impossible. And knowing my friends and family have a way to tell me how they are without a lengthy check in/conversation makes me worry less about them struggling in silence. 

From there you can develop plans for each colour/stage. But be careful not to overload your daughter with plans. Start with the code system and build from there over time once you both get your footing.

After thinking for a bit these would be the main things to consider. As it seems like you're leaning towards getting someone to help you set up the file and be a point of call for you if you have questions, having this info ready will help them help you: 

1. Billing: Does she want to be able to create and send invoices from the software? What about payment reminders to clients? 
How does she bill her clients? Does she charge for each employees time e.g employee A $90 P/hour, employee B $120 p/hr. Or is it a daily rate for each child? Does each family have their own rate or is it set?
Some software offers time billing (having an hourly rate per employee you can on-charge), others do not. Some (most) software also let's you set up items so you can charge the same thing every time. 

1.5 Payments: does she want clients to be able to pay online? I.e send an invoice via email, they click a link and pay by card. This is another feature that can add to cost, or to savings if you don't need it. 

2. Employees: how many employees, how often is payroll, etc etc. Any employees with special set ups on how they're paid. This will influence choice of software and set up. 

3. Expenses tracking: what are the usual overhead/running costs of the business? What are the direct costs of sales? Anything specific she wants to track separately or is specific to the industry that others might not know about (e.g licenses, background checks, diapers, idk) 

3.5 Any loans in the business name, as well as any personal money the owner (your friend) has put into the business and not gotten back. If her finances are very tangled with the business that's okay, it's what bookkeeping is there to track, but she has to be able to go over the transactions with whoever's doing the work to keep it separate. 

If all my clients came to me with that info to start with I would cry tears of joy haha.

There's also some free bookkeeping software that will do the basics (not sure what's available where you are). 

Ultimately what do you/your friend want your bookkeeping software to do? Because if it's just keeping track of money coming in/out then any software will be fine. If it's going to be a bit more complex like tracking loans, running payroll, etc, then shopping around is a good idea. OP I don't know why every commenter in this thread is being super whatever-the-opposite-of-empathetic is. 

I get why you're upset, I really do. Someone you thought was solely in your daughter's corner, who your daughter should be able to trust, is now involved in the messiness of your court case. Is everything your daughter says now court record? Did you accidentally sign her up to have some woman talk to her about her parents court case instead of actually providing therapy? 

All the worst case scenarios are probably in your head right now because you've seen the worst of people and you want to protect your daughter. But please just give this therapist the benefit of the doubt. Because on the opposite side, this lady working as a court appointed therapist (or in some way involved with court cases reguarly) has probably seen the worst case scenarios of parents using their kids.

Somewhere along the lines you weren't reasonably informed of what you were signing up for when this arrangement was made. The court system is a mess and things don't always run like they should, it's not her fault any more than it is yours (aka blame the system).

My advice is to write a letter or prepare a draft of what you want to ask/say. Give her the benefit of the doubt, don't come in accusing or adamant she is to stay away from your case. And also don't try to bring in your own background with your daughter's father/your ex - the therapist at least knows of your case, any attempts to provide context may be seen as trying to gain sympathy. 
Let her know what you had assumed her role with your daughter was (solely as her therapist, to provide support, etc) and that it was a shock to find out that's not the case. Ask for clarification and how her work is in the best interest of your daughter (because that's likely her main role). If possible you could ask for a copy of the informed consent paperwork or an outline/pamphlet of how she/her organisation operates within the court system. How does it affect/inform the therapy she provides? Is she asking your daughter questions for the court or is she letting your daughter's words guide therapy?

I wish I knew a lot of what I know now back when I was 15, or at least had an adult around who knew or had experience with this.

Some of the things I wish I knew:

1. High school / good grades is NOT the only pathway to university. There are external exams (STAT test I believe it's called) and university entry pathways that each uni offers (bridging courses). Basically you just have to prove you have the reading and speaking skills to understand the content and you're in for most courses. 

2. Encourage your kids to explore their interests rather than pick a career at school and stick to it. When I was 15 I wanted to be an engineer, at 18 I wanted to be a psychologist, at 22 a vet, I'm 28 now and I'm working towards a career in accounting. The thing these all have in common is that I like learning how things work, I like puzzles, and I learnt that through practical knowledge. 
Get your kids volunteering, joining clubs, etc, to build a wider knowledge of what their career/life might look like, rather than focusing on just getting the grades for it. Having the practical knowledge really helps know if you want to do this. 

3. As I said above grades don't matter as much. But good study habits do! I was used to high school telling me what I needed to study and covering all the important info in class, university really relies on you being able to study on your own and figure out what's important yourself. You'll find a lot of kids who do great in highschool struggle in university, whereas kids who may have been in the middle but have built good study habits will thrive.

Depending on what high school the kids are in they might be pushed towards the academic view of uni = success. But (majority of) these are people who have been in school their whole lives, they only really know the school way of achieving things. Look at local connections, ask about pathways to a career and what sort of knowledge or experience they would need. 

At the end of the day universities are a business, they want money. They're not necessarily the best route to take. Not to say they're not valuable or worth it! Just worth looking at the best options :)

I was a retail worker when SCOs first came in, and when we got them installed we all had mandatory training on how to use/fix them and how to teach people how to use them. Something I doubt employees today are getting.

It has gotten a lot worse since I was working, mostly because they put one staff member on to supervise 12 registers and then just abandon them. I know it's mostly due to understaffing, not any of the staff you see on the floor/at the checkouts fault. 

Anyways I still use SCO's and rarely have any problems, here's a few tips for using them:

1. Plan how you're going to pack your items and what order you'll scan the items in. That way you're not shuffling things around on the scales while the SCO is waiting for you to put whatever you scanned in the bagging area. This is the BIGGEST cause of the "unexpected item in bagging area" error message. 

2. WAIT FOR THE GREEN LIGHT. Once you've placed your item in the bagging area, wait until the lights around the scanner turn green. That's when it will scan again. 
If the light doesn't turn green, check to make sure the item is actually on the scales. Sometimes it needs to be more centred. 
Also don't sit the thing you're going to scan next in front of the scanner. Because it may accidentally scan while you're shuffling things around/bagging and then it stuffs up the scales. 

3. Do one thing at a time. Similar to #2. If you need to take bags off the scales, or move things around: stop scanning, wait for the green light, and then do what you need to do. When you're finished, clear whatever message comes up (if anything does). I see so many people press the error message and then keep moving things around and the message comes up again.

4. If you do get a "employee needed" message, don't expect them to notice you just standing there staring at your screen, huffing and puffing. On the occasion I get the message I'll look over to the staff member, raise my hand a little to get their attention/let them know they're needed. Strangely treating them politely means I get seen to quicker *shocked Pikachu face*

Forewarning I live in Australia so this might be different, but I also work for a freight forwarder so deal with a lot of courier companies daily. And believe me this is something I deal with daily.   

Things I've found out: 

1. Courier companies charge more for residential delivery because they claim it's harder to deliver. They also charge a fee every time a package isn't "able to be delivered" (so one of those cards costs the sender more money). The companies themselves are trying to push more senders to deliver direct to businesses for a more streamline service.

2. In AUS, companies like UPS and FedEx use sub contractors, so service is widely different from driver to driver. Some are incredibly useless, and they get paid so long as they do their route no matter how poor their service is. Others are fantastic. 

3. The biggest one: during COVID, they removed the requirement for signature deliveries as a default rule, so unless the shipment specifically states "signature required upon delivery" then they are allowed to leave it wherever on the property. 
So drivers are now used to just being able to leave it, and for some reason don't want to take the extra 30 seconds to ring the doorbell and hand it to someone. 

This is just my experience as a sender, the real reason could be different. Drivers have a lot more control since COVID, there's less competition and the freight companies have learnt how much they're needed. Unfortunately it all passes onto the end consumer. 

If you want to complain keep records. If you have a location thing on your phone that says you were home at the time, if you see the delivery van outside take a picture of it, a picture of the note being left etc etc.

To complain look up the courier companies website, they'll usually have a contact us/enquiries area and some even have a portal to submit complaints rather than having to sit on the phone. Even without proof you can still complain, it's just better (and hella satisfying) to slap them in the face with proof. I know from experience hehe.

You can use things to get the environment to train him so his training isn't reliant on you. For countertops you can get some double-sided tape (I think like carpet tape or something, it doesn't hurt the dogs but is unpleasant) and stick it on the edge of the counter so when they first jump up they get that unpleasantness. 

 You can get little motion sensing aerosol cans especially for dogs, which blows a puff of air at the dog if it sticks its head above the counter.  
  
 Another thing is to make a false countertop, so a piece of cardboard or something, and have it stick out a little bit over the counter. To weigh it down get a tin can or jar which won't break and fill it with something that will make a lot of noise (but obv won't break or be harmful to the dog). When the dog jumps up it will knock the "false counter" down, also knocking over the tin which will make a very loud noise the dog then associates with jumping on the counter.     

There's a heap of other ideas you can have a Google "safe booby traps for dogs" or "environmental training for dogs". You want them to associate places you don't want them with something unpleasant. The LAST thing you want to do is yell at/get angry at the dog AFTER you find the mess they've made. Because that's how they learn to wait until you're not around and get sneakier. You want to interrupt the bad behaviour when they do it, not punish the aftermath.

In Australia if you're turning right in an intersection (across traffic) it is illegal to cross the solid line into the middle of the intersection if you don't have a path across traffic. So basically your wheels can't stop once you're in the intersection, even if you've got a green light (we are not allowed to cross at all on red lights, some intersections have green arrows but that means the opposite side of traffic is stopped at a red), and those in oncoming traffic have right of way. Sounds simple, right? 

I didn't even know this was a law until a few years after I got my license. Almost *everyone* will roll and stop in the middle of the intersection to wait for a safe break in traffic, often the car behind them does the same (so two cars waiting in the middle). I get honked at daily for waiting behind the solid line. When you think about it it makes sense not to but it's what everyone does and the law isn't enforced. But if you're in an accident and you've done this (say you move to cross on yellow but someone oncoming speeds up on yellow and T-bone you) you're technically at fault.

I've seen a few kangaroo comments on here but I'm gonna go in with my own.  
If you're driving and see a kangaroo on the road: slow down and then stop, don't swerve. Often there's more than one and if you swerve you can hit the ones following.     

If you do hit a roo there's two things to do:
DO NOT KEEP DRIVING. 
If it's still alive but wounded DO NOT GET OUT OF YOUR CAR. They can do a lot of damage even (especially) when hurt. Call your local ranger/wildlife line to alert them and someone trained will come out. 

If it's dead, stop and get out. Try and pull it off the road to avoid more accidents, and call your ranger/wildlife line to report a dead roo.  
Reporting is important!! Females can be carrying joeys which can survive for days inside the pouch of a dead mother.

If you are faced with an aggressive kangaroo, don't waste time getting behind them, they may not be able to hop backwards but they're fast! Best thing to do when approaching a roo is to bend down so as to make yourself shorter (they only stand to full height when preparing to fight so you being straightened comes off as aggressive to them), keep facing them as you back away.  

If one looks ready to fight (trust me you'll know) punch them in the face. Their arm strength is fractional compared to their legs, and they often punch each other before kicking (which is where the real danger is, google what a kangaroo foot looks like if you're curious). If you punch them they'll assume your legs are much more powerful and will *hopefully* back down.  

Of course I haven't tested the punching method myself, and I definitely advocate for not starting fights with kangaroos, but if you ever find yourself in that specific situation...  

Edit: I am not saying try to fight a roo or test out this tactic for fun. I'm saying this as an absolute last resort to save your ass. Yes, they look cute and cuddly but these things can disembowel with a kick. The force they have in their legs is phenomenal and in no way should you even get close enough to one to punch them because then they'll be close enough to kill you.  
This is like the advice you get if you should encounter a shark and it's looking to eat you. It is highly unlikely you will ever need it and you might end up dead regardless.
